findings.summary: A whitespace-only difference does not defeat patch-id matching, because git patch-id ignores whitespace by default.
findings.evidence: "One edited line, one whitespace fix = ==no match==" — git-patch-id(1): `--unstable` is the default and "whitespace is ignored"; only `--verbatim` (or `patchid.verbatim=true`) keeps whitespace significant.
findings.fix: Drop the whitespace example: "One edited line (conflict resolution, a rebase fixup) = ==no match==; pure whitespace changes are ignored by patch-id unless `patchid.verbatim` is set."

findings.summary: `revert` is used in the comparison table and in a full command example before the handbook ever says what revert does; its definition arrives only in the page's closing callout.
findings.evidence: Page 4 opens with the table "Axis | merge | pick | revert" ("auditability | good | poor w/o `-x` | **best**") and later runs "git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>"; the only definition appears in the last block: "==Revert== on anything already pushed — it adds the inverse diff and deletes nothing."
findings.fix: Add revert to page 3's "1. What Each Tool Does" bullets — "==Revert==: new commit applying the inverse diff; deletes nothing, safe on shared branches" — so the trade-off table and the `-m 1` merge-revert example on page 4 land on a defined term.

findings.summary: The bisect chapter's closing summary is stranded on page 7 after the reflog chapter has already opened on page 6, so the numbered sections run 1 (reflog) then 5 (bisect) then 2 (reflog).
findings.evidence: Page 6 ends with "1. What Reflog Is" — "==git reflog== (short for `git reflog show HEAD`) lists __every position HEAD has held__"; page 7 then opens with "5. Summary" / "0 good · 1-127 bad · **125 skip** — the whole contract." before returning to "$ git reflog" and "2. Selectors: @{n} vs ~n".
findings.fix: Move the bisect "5. Summary" checkbox block to the end of page 6, immediately after the "Reading a fuzzy result" tip, and start the reflog chapter ("1. What Reflog Is") at the top of page 7 so the reflog sections run 1→5 uninterrupted.

findings.summary: Unrendered colour markup leaks into the body text of section 1's bullet list, showing raw template syntax instead of styled text.
findings.evidence: Bullet reads "Pick the {green:HEAD@{1}} entry whose reason is commit, not commit (amend)" — the literal braces and "green:" directive are printed on the page.
findings.fix: Fix the inline-colour directive in the source bullet so it renders as green-styled `HEAD@{1}`; the nested `{` in `HEAD@{1}` is breaking the parser, so escape it or switch that span to a plain code span.

findings.summary: The "hard rule" wrongly says work that was never committed or stashed is unrecoverable, when staged (`git add`ed) content survives as dangling blobs.
findings.evidence: "Reflog journals ==refs==, not files. Work never committed or stashed is **gone** — no command brings it back." — but page 8 itself lists "`fsck --lost-found` | dangling objects" and "An aborted commit no ref ever held is fsck's job, not reflog's."
findings.fix: Qualify it: "Work never **staged**, committed or stashed is gone. Anything you ran `git add` on still exists as a blob — `git fsck --lost-found` then `git show <blob>` gets it back."

findings.summary: The claim that `git gc --prune=now` destroys the recovery window is wrong, because gc treats reflog-referenced objects as reachable.
findings.evidence: "`git gc --prune=now` destroys the recovery window" (bullet under "3. Reflog Mistakes"), which also contradicts page 8's own kill-switch callout: "only run it right before a genuine `gc --prune=now`".
findings.fix: Reword to: "`git gc --prune=now` only deletes objects unreachable from refs *and* reflogs — your reset from five minutes ago survives it. It destroys the window only after `git reflog expire --expire-unreachable=now --all`."

findings.summary: The decorative pushpin graphic on sticky notes is positioned on top of the last characters of a code line in several code blocks.
findings.evidence: Page 6: pin sits over the tail of "node -e 'assert(cart.total()==9)'"; page 2: pin sits over "# '+' = missing, '-' = already there"; page 5: pin sits between "git bisect" and "fast" in "git bisect slow; git bisect fast".
findings.fix: Offset the pin anchor so it sits in the note's top margin above the code line, or shift the note/pin right of the longest code line in the block.

findings.summary: The defaults table says `git gc --prune=now` applies to "all loose" objects, when it only prunes loose objects that are unreachable from refs and reflogs.
findings.evidence: Table row: "git gc --prune=now | instant | all loose".
findings.fix: Change the "Applies to" cell to "unreachable loose" (and ideally note it still respects reflog entries).

findings.summary: A loose branch ref file is 41 bytes, not 40, and packed branches have no file at all.
findings.evidence: "A ==branch== is a 40-byte file holding one SHA."
findings.fix: Say "a one-line file holding one 40-char SHA (41 bytes with the newline) — or a line in `.git/packed-refs`".

findings.summary: The "Touches" column labels the three tools patch / history / pointers before that three-layer model is introduced, which happens in a callout on page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 1 table rows "I want this change here | cherry-pick | patch", "Which change broke it | bisect | history", "Where did my commit go | reflog | pointers"; the explanation "Three layers: ==patches== (content diffs, cherry-pick) vs ==pointers== (refs, reflog) vs ==history== (the DAG, bisect)" is the "Mental model for the book" callout on page 2.
findings.fix: Move the "Mental model for the book" callout to page 1, directly above the Question/Tool/Touches table, so the column header is defined before it is used.

findings.summary: Page 1 closes with a gc/reflog-expiry defaults table although neither `gc` nor reachability has been explained; the lifecycle that motivates the table is on page 2.
findings.evidence: Page 1 final table: "gc.reflogExpire | 90 days | reachable", "...ExpireUnreachable | 30 days | orphans", "git gc --prune=now | instant | all loose" — while the chain diagram "Life of an orphaned commit" ("unreachable, still there" → "gc after expiry deletes it") is the first block of page 2.
findings.fix: Swap the two: put the "Reachable vs existing" chain diagram at the end of page 1 and move the expiry-defaults table after it (the same table is repeated on page 7, where the reflog chapter can carry the numbers).

findings.summary: The page-2 title names only cherry-pick, but the page opens with three blocks about object reachability and gc that the title does not cover.
findings.evidence: page_title "Cherry-pick: Replaying a Commit" sits above the chain diagram "Life of an orphaned commit" ("reset --hard: no branch reaches it" → "gc after expiry deletes it"), the takeaway "Mental model for the book", and the callout "Terminology trap" ("'Lost commits' are __not lost__ until `git gc` runs"); the first cherry-pick heading, "1. What It Does", is the fourth block.
findings.fix: Use the deck's own compound-title style (as on page 4, "Revert, Duplicates and Bisect Setup") — retitle page 2 to "Unreachable vs Gone, and Cherry-pick" so the opening reachability/gc section is described.

findings.summary: A forward reference points at the page it is printed on, so the learner is sent to a page they are already reading.
findings.evidence: Page 3 callout "Copy, not move": "The source commit is untouched; the patch now exists **twice** under two SHAs. Page 3 covers what that costs you."
findings.fix: Change the sentence to point at the material that actually follows: "The rest of this page and the next cover what that costs you."

findings.summary: Dropped stash entries are not recoverable from `refs/stash`, since `git stash drop` removes the entry from that reflog.
findings.evidence: "Dropped stash: entries live under `refs/stash`", listed as a rescue recipe alongside "Truly orphaned stash: `git fsck --unreachable`".
findings.fix: Reword to: "Stash stack = the reflog of `refs/stash` (`git stash list`); a **dropped** entry is removed from it — recover it with `git fsck --unreachable | grep commit` and `git stash apply <sha>`."

findings.summary: A literal tab escape sequence is printed inside the sticky note on the "Storage On Disk" code block.
findings.evidence: Note reads "plain append-only text: old new who when\treason" — `\t` appears as two characters between "when" and "reason".
findings.fix: Replace the `\t` in the note text with a real space or separator (e.g. "old new who when reason").

findings.summary: `git fsck` is prescribed as a rescue step on page 7 with no statement of what it does; what fsck finds and how it differs from the reflog is only explained on page 8.
findings.evidence: Page 7 recipe "git fsck --unreachable|grep commit" and bullet "Truly orphaned stash: `git fsck --unreachable`"; the explanation arrives on page 8: "`fsck --lost-found` | dangling objects | which ref owned them".
findings.fix: Add one clause where fsck first appears on page 7 — e.g. "`git fsck --unreachable` scans .git/objects directly for commits no ref points at" — or move the "Reflog vs fsck" comparison table up to precede the rescue recipes.

findings.summary: An escaped table-cell pipe is printed literally in the "Four More Playbooks" recovery column.
findings.evidence: Row "Deleted merged branch" shows recovery "git reflog \| grep feat/x finds last checkout" — the backslash before the pipe is visible.
findings.fix: Unescape the pipe when rendering table cells, or rewrite the cell to avoid a pipe (e.g. `git reflog` piped to `grep feat/x`).
